Bounded queues and careful recovery

A queue separates accepting work from completing it. That separation is useful only when both sides understand the resource budget. An unbounded queue can hide a slow consumer until memory becomes the limiting resource, while a bounded queue makes admission an explicit decision. A producer needs an answer when capacity is exhausted.

Preserve the contract

Consider a collector that refreshes many independent subscriptions. Its network requests may take seconds, even though switching the selected article should remain interactive. Moving collection away from the input loop removes that direct dependency. It does not make requests faster, so measurement and honest failure reporting remain part of the design. Keep the last useful result when a request fails. 

fn admit<T>(item: T) -> Result<T, T> {
    Ok(item)
}

Durable identity matters when results arrive later. Capture the article identity and URL before submitting a request, then validate both again before committing. A change in selection must never redirect a completed result into a different article. The same rule applies to a passage captured before opening a private note editor. 

SELECT body
FROM article_documents
WHERE article_id = 42;

Transactions provide a useful boundary between a downloaded document and its search index. Readers should see a complete previous version or a complete replacement. Personal notes and the original feed remain independent from this cache, which makes recovery and source comparison possible without losing the reader's work.

ResourcePolicy
QueueBounded admission
CachePreserve on failure

Follow the recovery reference for a second worked example. Tests should assert preserved data and credible failure behavior, rather than merely confirming that a method was called. Benchmarks should separate setup from the work being measured and check the returned result on every iteration.
